one_liner: Tencent's Rust QUIC/HTTP3 library with C API: ~2.4x quiche on request and stream-churn rate, slower on bulk.
what_it_does: TQUIC implements IETF QUIC v1 and HTTP/3. It adds pluggable congestion control (CUBIC, BBR, BBRv3, COPA) and Multipath QUIC. It is sans-IO: your code owns the UDP sockets, feeds datagrams to an Endpoint (recv), then calls process_connections and on_timeout. The Endpoint owns every connection, routes packets by connection ID, tracks timers, and calls back into a TransportHandler (conn created/established/closed, stream readable/writable/closed) and a PacketSendHandler, which receives outgoing packets in batches. C and C++ programs use the cbindgen-generated include/tquic.h (quic_endpoint_*, quic_conn_*, quic_stream_*), built with --features ffi. It is not API-compatible with quiche, which gives you one Connection object per peer and leaves routing and timer bookkeeping to the application.
how_it_is_fast: Connections live in a slab indexed through FxHash CID routing tables. Each process_connections pass touches only connections marked 'tickable', meaning they have pending events. It then round-robins over 'sendable' connections and writes packets into a reusable buffer pool. Those packets go to the application's send callback in batches (send_batch_size, default 64), which fits sendmmsg-style I/O. Timers for all connections share one double-ended priority queue, and streams use FxHashMap indexes, bitflag state and per-urgency send queues. Neither TQUIC nor quicperf says which of these explains the ~2.4x request-rate gap over quiche, so the cause is not documented. The design shows no advantage on bulk-transfer paths.
when_to_use: Single-threaded QUIC servers that handle many small request/response exchanges on fresh streams. quicperf measured 155k rps for TQUIC vs 119k for LSQUIC and 64.6k for quiche on one pinned server thread.
Workloads that open and close many short streams, such as RPC-style stream churn or close/reset cleanup: about 178k streams/s vs about 75k for quiche.
High-rate 0-RTT request/response after session resumption: 154k vs 65k rps for quiche.
You want a Rust QUIC stack with a C API that already handles CID routing, per-connection timers and send batching, so you don't have to write that code around quiche.
You need Multipath QUIC, BBRv3/COPA, or mobile targets (Android, iOS and HarmonyOS builds are documented).
when_not_to_use: Bulk transfer. In the same run TQUIC downloaded at 8.6 Gbps vs quiche 11.3, LSQUIC 16.4 and ngtcp2 18.2 Gbps, and it lost to quiche on every upload, bidirectional, multistream, loss-recovery and flow-control row (0.76-0.96x).

Unreliable DATAGRAMs (RFC 9221). They are not in develop or release v1.6.0 (issue #222 still open) and exist only on feature branches. Even the feature-branch build managed 0.89M vs 5.1M DATAGRAMs/s for quiche.
Workloads dominated by resumed connections: 216 vs 301 conn/s for quiche (syscall backend).

Memory-tight servers holding many idle connections: 146.6 KB vs 125.4 KB of RSS per idle connection compared with quiche (syscall). Issue #494 (tquic_server OOM-killed while serving a 30 MB file) is still open, and its fix PR #498 was closed without merging.
Full HTTP/3 feature coverage. The QPACK dynamic table is a TODO in qpack.rs (#225), and ECN (#224), QUIC v2 (#221), HTTP/3 trailers (#226) and async APIs (#23) are missing.

integration.form: crate; also static lib and shared lib (crate-type lib/staticlib/cdylib, C API enabled with --features ffi, header include/tquic.h)
integration.dependencies: BoringSSL (vendored git submodule built via CMake, or a prebuilt one via BORINGSSL_LIB_DIR); Rust crates ring, bytes, slab, rustc-hash, priority-queue, smallvec, lru, brotli, flate2 and others; optional serde (qlog feature) and sfv (h3 feature)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.70 (Cargo rust-version), but the repo pins 1.90.0 in rust-toolchain.toml after recent toolchain breakages; the docs also require GCC 9.3+, CMake 3.22+ and git 2.0+
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, Windows, iOS, Android and HarmonyOS per the docs; open issues report no exported C symbols in the Windows static lib (#484) and a build failure on Apple M1 (#447)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. In Rust the Endpoint holds Rc<RefCell<..>> and Rc<dyn PacketSendHandler>, which makes it !Send. Treat each endpoint as confined to one thread and scale with one endpoint per thread/core. The FFI adds no locking.

gotchas: A packet-generation error on one connection makes process_connections return Err for the whole endpoint, and the remaining connections are not processed on that pass. Issue #459 reports repeated InternalError under 1.5-2 Gbps load.

The library does no GSO or sendmmsg itself. Each outgoing packet is a separate Vec<u8> in the batch handed to on_packets_send, so the batching only pays off if your callback does vectored or segmented sends.
tquic.h #includes openssl/ssl.h and exposes SSL_CTX (quic_tls_config_new_with_ssl_ctx). C/C++ consumers need BoringSSL headers and must link the same BoringSSL build as TQUIC.

The benchmarked build (50f5a55) is a DATAGRAM feature-branch commit, 1 ahead of and 3 behind develop. The published crate (v1.6.0, Feb 2025) cannot reproduce the DATAGRAM rows. quic_set_logger at TRACE level is reported to crash (#500).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick TQUIC over ngtcp2, LSQUIC or picoquic when one server thread must handle as many small requests or short streams as possible. In the same quicperf run it served 155k rps vs 119k for LSQUIC, 59k for picoquic and 51k for ngtcp2. Pick ngtcp2 or LSQUIC for bulk throughput (about 2x TQUIC's download rate), and quiche for DATAGRAM rate or resumed connects.
verified_claims_summary: quicperf is an independent C++ loopback harness: one pinned server thread, 16 client threads, CUBIC, TLS 1.3 through a shared BoringSSL build, p50 of 20 samples. In it, TQUIC at feature-branch commit 50f5a55 reached 2.36-2.40x quiche 0.29.0 on request/response, stream churn, small messages, 0-RTT and close/reset with the syscall backend. With io_uring the ratio was 3.0-3.4x, partly because quiche's own io_uring rows are slower than its syscall rows. TQUIC lost on every bulk row (0.76-0.96x), on resumed connect (0.72x) and on DATAGRAM rate (0.17x). Both libraries were built with -C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3 and fat LTO; the CPU model is not recorded and the run came from a harness working tree with uncommitted changes.
status_note: Apache-2.0 (includes BSD/MIT-derived code) and usable as a vendored crate or static lib. Despite the 'active' label, there has been no release since v1.6.0 (2025-02-25), and develop has seen only toolchain fixes since August 2025 (last commit 2025-12-23).
